table.text: In order to participate in our studies, volunteers had to be native or near-native German (both studies) or French (Study 2) speakers and had to have normal or corrected-to-normal hearing levels and vision.
A total of 𝑁 = 83 volunteers signed up for participation in Study 1, of whom 21 had to be excluded from analysis.
A total of 𝑁 = 209 volunteers signed up for Study 2, of whom 70 had to be excluded from analysis.
General procedure Volunteers signed up for participation via email or through our participant management system.

Participants were allowed to complete sessions at their preferred time of day, but were instructed to take each session at about the same time of day, in the same quiet environment, and on the same device (computer or tablet; no smartphones).
After each training and test run, participants were informed about their average accuracy during the previous run.
Participants were allowed to take a short break before continuing with the next task.
Finally, the participants were debriefed and compensated.

Pre-screening questionnaire Upon signing up for participation, volunteers completed a prescreening questionnaire in which they were asked about their age, level of education, current occupation, and language skills.

In this questionnaire, participants were also asked to disclose the current presence of neurological or psychiatric disorders (namely epilepsy, depression, schizophrenia), attention or memory deficits, hearing or vision impairments, sleep disorders, or irregular sleep schedules, e.g., due to shift work.

Participants were told that in this experiment they must learn to categorize monsters called "Fernis" into two families, the "Brigus" and the "Sidors" that have distinctive sets of visual and auditory features.

Participants were instructed to try to identify the relevant features and feature combinations that define each monster family during training runs in order to maximize their categorization accuracy during both training and test runs.
Participants had to indicate the family of the monster on display by clicking on the button of the corresponding family (Fig. 1).

> Participants were allowed to take a short break before continuing with the next task.

> Finally, the participants were debriefed and compensated.

> Pre-screening questionnaire Upon signing up for participation, volunteers completed a prescreening questionnaire in which they were asked about their age, level of education, current occupation, and language skills.

> In this questionnaire, participants were also asked to disclose the current presence of neurological or psychiatric disorders (namely epilepsy, depression, schizophrenia), attention or memory deficits, hearing or vision impairments, sleep disorders, or irregular sleep schedules, e.g., due to shift work.

> Participants were told that in this experiment they must learn to categorize monsters called "Fernis" into two families, the "Brigus" and the "Sidors" that have distinctive sets of visual and auditory features.

> Participants were instructed to try to identify the relevant features and feature combinations that define each monster family during training runs in order to maximize their categorization accuracy during both training and test runs.

> Participants had to indicate the family of the monster on display by clicking on the button of the corresponding family (Fig. 1).

> In this test, we first examined whether participants were able to recall the defining feature values of each monster family.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 4928 columns across 308 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 308 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: In both studies, participants had to learn to distinguish between two families of cartoon monsters, i.e., the "concepts", in daily experimental sessions over five consecutive days (Fig. 1 A and D).

In order to participate in our studies, volunteers had to be native or near-native German (both studies) or French (Study 2) speakers and had to have normal or corrected-to-normal hearing levels and vision.
A total of 𝑁 = 83 volunteers signed up for participation in Study 1, of whom 21 had to be excluded from analysis.
A total of 𝑁 = 209 volunteers signed up for Study 2, of whom 70 had to be excluded from analysis.
General procedure Volunteers signed up for participation via email or through our participant management system.

Participants were allowed to complete sessions at their preferred time of day, but were instructed to take each session at about the same time of day, in the same quiet environment, and on the same device (computer or tablet; no smartphones).
After each training and test run, participants were informed about their average accuracy during the previous run.
Participants were allowed to take a short break before continuing with the next task.
Finally, the participants were debriefed and compensated.

Pre-screening questionnaire Upon signing up for participation, volunteers completed a prescreening questionnaire in which they were asked about their age, level of education, current occupation, and language skills.

In this questionnaire, participants were also asked to disclose the current presence of neurological or psychiatric disorders (namely epilepsy, depression, schizophrenia), attention or memory deficits, hearing or vision impairments, sleep disorders, or irregular sleep schedules, e.g., due to shift work.

Participants were told that in this experiment they must learn to categorize monsters called "Fernis" into two families, the "Brigus" and the "Sidors" that have distinctive sets of visual and auditory features.

Participants were instructed to try to identify the relevant features and feature combinations that define each monster family during training runs in order to maximize their categorization accuracy during both training and test runs.
Participants had to indicate the family of the monster on display by clicking on the button of the corresponding family (Fig. 1).
In this test, we first examined whether participants were able to recall the defining feature values of each monster family.
For each value, participants had to indicate the corresponding family by clicking the respective button on the screen.
In this version, participants were told that they would compete against six other participants who were also performing the task.
However, participants were misled into believing that their opponents were actual human participants.
Participants were told that they would compete against one of these opponents during each training run, but that they would compete against all six opponents at once during test runs.
Participants were told that they would see their own score and the opponent's score after each trial.

Before each test run, participants were informed that they would now have to compete against all six opponents, that no feedback would be presented after a response, but that a leaderboard would be shown at the end.
In Study 1, half of participants were subjected to a gamified version of the concept learning task, in which they had to compete against other virtual participants during training and testing.
Written consent was obtained from all individuals prior to their participation.
After the final session, participants completed a feature-knowledge test assessing recall and recognition of category-defining feature values.

Participants were recruited from the body of German-speaking (both studies) and French-speaking (Study 2) bachelor's students in psychology at UniDistance Suisse, Switzerland, as well as from the general population (Study 1 only).

report: #### MATLAB code, no reproducible output

4 MATLAB code files are present, but this module has no way to extract statistics from MATLAB output, and no self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, a Stata output log, or Mplus output) was found to fall back on. Readers without a MATLAB license cannot currently see what the code produced. Consider depositing the results as well, so they are visible without MATLAB installed: run `diary('output.txt')` (or `diary on`) before the analysis and `diary off` after to save a plain-text transcript of everything printed to the Command Window, or use `publish('script.m', 'pdf')` (or the Live Editor's Export/Save As) to generate a single readable document with the code, its output, and any figures together.

text.text: Conceptual knowledge allows us to make sense of new events and helps guide decisions in novel situations.
But how conceptual knowledge is acquired and represented is still poorly understood.
One view holds that humans merely memorize a collection of specific examples to represent a concept.
An alternative view proposes that humans gradually integrate past experiences into abstract prototypes to represent concepts.
Importantly, the process of integration and abstraction has been theorized to occur offline -especially during rest and sleep.
But direct evidence for an offline integration is scarce.

By fitting cognitive models of concept learning to behavioral data from two longitudinal concept learning studies, we find that prototype models explain behavior better than exemplar models from the earliest assessment, and that this advantage increases further across offline intervals between experimental sessions.

We further show that these offline increases in prototype dominance are observed when concept learning builds on few examples and requires distinguishing relevant from irrelevant features in perceptually complex, naturalistic stimuli.
These findings provide novel insights into how humans distill unique experiences into abstract generalizable knowledge about the world.

Concepts provide abstract generalized information about the world that allows us to make sense of new situations and helps guide our behavior in unfamiliar settings.
Throughout our lives, we accumulate a large corpus of conceptual knowledge that enables us to navigate our complex world.
The scale of this corpus is illustrated by the fact that by the age of 20, an average adult knows over 40'000 words for distinct concepts [1].
text.formatted: The scale of this corpus is illustrated by the fact that by the age of 20, an average adult knows over 40'000 words for distinct concepts <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: But how individual concepts are formed and stored to build such a large corpus of knowledge is still poorly understood.
Conceptual knowledge allows people to generalize from past experiences to new situations [2] [3] [4] [5], but how individual concepts are represented remains debated [6] [7] [8].
text.formatted: Conceptual knowledge allows people to generalize from past experiences to new situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>, but how individual concepts are represented remains debated <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: According to exemplar theories, concepts are represented through memories of specific events or examples: the "exemplars."
New events are categorized as members of that concept based on their similarity to memorized exemplars [9] [10] [11] [12].
text.formatted: New events are categorized as members of that concept based on their similarity to memorized exemplars <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Prototype theories, on the other hand, assume that humans integrate past experiences into an abstract prototype representation and categorize new events based on their resemblance to this prototype [13] [14] [15] [16] [17].
text.formatted: Prototype theories, on the other hand, assume that humans integrate past experiences into an abstract prototype representation and categorize new events based on their resemblance to this prototype <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Both theories have found support in the literature [18, 19], and some work suggests that both types of representations may coexist in the brain [20, 21].
text.formatted: Both theories have found support in the literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19]</ref>, and some work suggests that both types of representations may coexist in the brain <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21]</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, the representational code of concepts was observed to change with the level of expertise, but findings on the direction of these changes are contradictory.
While some studies suggested that concept representations shift from prototypes to exemplars from novice to expert [22, 23], other work reported changes in the opposite direction [21, 24].
text.formatted: While some studies suggested that concept representations shift from prototypes to exemplars from novice to expert <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23]</ref>, other work reported changes in the opposite direction <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24]</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, how concept representations form and change over time has never been investigated in long-term studies that examine concept learning over multiple sessions and days.
Concepts are often learned and refined over long periods of time, sometimes throughout an individual's entire life span.
Importantly, several theories posit that conceptual knowledge forms offline, especially during periods of rest and sleep [25] [26] [27] [28] [29] [30].
text.formatted: Importantly, several theories posit that conceptual knowledge forms offline, especially during periods of rest and sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: During rest, the fast-learning hippocampus, which memorizes individual events and episodes, repeatedly reactivates and replays memories of recently experienced episodes [31] [32] [33].
text.formatted: During rest, the fast-learning hippocampus, which memorizes individual events and episodes, repeatedly reactivates and replays memories of recently experienced episodes <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: This replay is proposed to strengthen episodic memories in the hippocampus [27, 34] and support the gradual formation and refinement of abstract, integrated representations in the slow-learning neocortex.
text.formatted: This replay is proposed to strengthen episodic memories in the hippocampus <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34]</ref> and support the gradual formation and refinement of abstract, integrated representations in the slow-learning neocortex.

text.text: In everyday life, conceptual knowledge may thus emerge through multiple cycles of learning followed by periods of memory transformation and abstraction during rest and sleep [35, 36].
text.formatted: In everyday life, conceptual knowledge may thus emerge through multiple cycles of learning followed by periods of memory transformation and abstraction during rest and sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36]</ref>.

text.text: Paradoxically, concept learning has so far mostly been studied on short time-scales -usually in single-session experiments.
Direct evidence for the offline integration of recent episodic memories into more abstract conceptual representations is scarce and inconclusive [37, 38].
text.formatted: Direct evidence for the offline integration of recent episodic memories into more abstract conceptual representations is scarce and inconclusive <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38]</ref>.

text.text: Our understanding of how concepts evolve over multiple cycles of learning and resting/sleep in naturalistic multi-day settings is thus still very limited.
In everyday life, concepts build on perceptually unique experiences that consist of highdimensional, multi-sensory perceptual information from which regularities need to be extracted.
Acquiring a novel concept thus involves integrating features across modalities [39] and learning to distinguish between diagnostic and non-diagnostic perceptual features [39] [40] [41].
text.formatted: Acquiring a novel concept thus involves integrating features across modalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref> and learning to distinguish between diagnostic and non-diagnostic perceptual features <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref>.

text.text: However, most studies to date have used highly simplified unimodal (usually visual) stimuli [8, 12] to study the emergence of conceptual knowledge.
text.formatted: However, most studies to date have used highly simplified unimodal (usually visual) stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref> to study the emergence of conceptual knowledge.

text.text: These stimuli only poorly reflect the distinctiveness and perceptual complexity of everyday experiences.
How concept representations form and evolve over time when they build on unique, multi-modal, high-dimensional experiences is largely undocumented.

We investigated how concepts are learned and how their mental representations evolve over multiple days and learning episodes when learning builds on highly distinctive, high-dimensional multimodal experiences.
We asked how accurately and rapidly participants generalize from training examples to novel items and whether conceptual knowledge evolves offline following learning events.
By fitting formal cognitive models of exemplar and prototype theories to behavior, we examined how mental representations of concepts change over time.
We further examined how the number of distinct training experiences influences concept learning.

Although concepts are thought to be formed by integrating multiple past experiences, much evidence suggests that humans can sometimes acquire concepts and learn to generalize to new situations from only very few examples [42, 43].
text.formatted: Although concepts are thought to be formed by integrating multiple past experiences, much evidence suggests that humans can sometimes acquire concepts and learn to generalize to new situations from only very few examples <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43]</ref>.

text.text: But such few-shot learning may promote different mental representations of a concept compared to learning that evolves over multiple distinct experiences.

Several studies indeed suggested that small sets of training examples promote exemplar representations, while larger training sets promote prototype-based processing and overall improve transfer to new items [14, [44] [45] [46].
text.formatted: Several studies indeed suggested that small sets of training examples promote exemplar representations, while larger training sets promote prototype-based processing and overall improve transfer to new items <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[45]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref>.

text.text: But other work found that training set size has little influence on internal representations and on the ability to generalize to new experiences [47] [48] [49].
text.formatted: But other work found that training set size has little influence on internal representations and on the ability to generalize to new experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[47]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[48]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[49]</ref>.

text.text: To examine how the number of distinct training examples influences concept learning and the evolution of concept representations, we compared learning from a small set of examples repeated many times with learning from a larger set repeated less frequently, while holding the total number of training presentations constant.
Finally, we asked how the perceptual distinctiveness of experiences influences concept learning.

Specifically, we examined how concept representations and the ability to generalize to new experiences evolve when learning builds on highly distinct stimuli that include both category-relevant and -irrelevant features compared to learning where stimuli only contain a limited set of features that are all relevant for categorization.

While some work suggested that high-dimensionality and the presence of non-diagnostic features promote prototype representations [13, 50, 51], other studies yielded evidence to the contrary [12, [52] [53] [54].
text.formatted: While some work suggested that high-dimensionality and the presence of non-diagnostic features promote prototype representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">50,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">51]</ref>, other studies yielded evidence to the contrary <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[52]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, all these findings were obtained in singlesession studies.

How conceptual knowledge forms and evolves online and offline over multiple days when it builds on highly distinctive, high-dimensional, multi-sensory experiences has, to the best of our knowledge, never been examined.
To investigate the long-term evolution of conceptual knowledge, we conducted two online studies using a family-resemblance category-learning task [55].
text.formatted: To investigate the long-term evolution of conceptual knowledge, we conducted two online studies using a family-resemblance category-learning task <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref>.

text.text: In both studies, participants had to learn to distinguish between two families of cartoon monsters, i.e., the "concepts", in daily experimental sessions over five consecutive days (Fig. 1 A and D).
text.formatted: In both studies, participants had to learn to distinguish between two families of cartoon monsters, i.e., the "concepts", in daily experimental sessions over five consecutive days (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">1 A</ref> and <ref type="figure">D</ref>).

text.text: In each session, participants practiced identifying the family of each item in the same set of training examples in six feedback-based training runs.

At the end of each session, and at the beginning of sessions 2-5, we assessed generalization by measuring participants' ability to categorize 64 test items that were never presented during training, without receiving feedback.
At the very end of the last session, we further examined participants' understanding of the learned concepts.

For this, we administered a feature knowledge test which first probed how well participants could recall the specific feature values associated with a concept, and then assessed their ability to recognize the concepts associated with every single feature value.
Concepts were defined by two prototype monsters with opposite values on each of eight diagnostic binary features, six of them visual, and two auditory (Fig. 1A).
text.formatted: Concepts were defined by two prototype monsters with opposite values on each of eight diagnostic binary features, six of them visual, and two auditory (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">1A</ref>).

text.text: From these prototypes, individual monsters with varying degrees of prototypicality were derived by inverting one, two, or three of the eight defining features to the value corresponding to the prototype of the opposite concept.
Monsters in the training set had a prototypicality of 75%, meaning that 6 out of the 8 binary features had the correct value of the corresponding prototype.
For the test items, prototypicality varied across 100%, 87.5%, 75%, and 62.5% (0 to 3 inverted features).
Monsters further varied on a set of non-diagnostic, category-irrelevant features that were counterbalanced across families.
Each monster thus had a highly distinctive visual and auditory appearance, which mimics the high perceptual distinctiveness and multi-dimensionality of everyday experiences.
In Study 1, we manipulated the training set size (small: 8 monsters; large: 24 monsters) as a between-subjects factor.
The total number of training presentations was held constant by repeating each example more frequently in the small-set condition.
We additionally manipulated the motivational context by using either a neutral task or a gamified concept learning task aimed at improving motivation and learning success (between-subjects factor).

Because the role of the motivational context is not within the scope of this work and had no significant impact on concept learning, the results on this manipulation are presented in the supplements only.
In Study 2, we aimed at replicating the key findings obtained in Study 1 for the small training set.

We further assessed the influence of the category-irrelevant, non-diagnostic features on concept learning by introducing an experimental condition in which stimuli contained only relevant, diagnostic features (between-subjects factor distinctiveness: high, i.e., with irrelevant features present, vs. low, i.e., relevant features only).
To examine the evolution of conceptual knowledge, we tracked how categorization accuracy and response latencies for training and test runs changed over time.

We further fit formal models of exemplar and prototype learning to behavior at test and quantified the relative support of prototypeversus exemplar-based representations as the difference in model fit errors between the prototype and exemplar models.
We refer to this measure as representational dominance, with positive values indicating greater exemplar dominance and negative values indicating greater prototype dominance.

To assess participants' understanding of the learned concepts at the end of the last session, we counted the number of feature values participants correctly recalled and associated with the corresponding monster family.
We further calculated the accuracy with which they could recognize the concept associated with each specific feature value.

Participants rapidly learned to categorize the training items and successfully generalized this learning to items not presented during training.

In both studies, participants categorized training and test items more accurately than expected by chance (50%) in every run, including the first session (one-sample t-tests; Study 1: 𝑡 (61) > 6, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 > 0.763; Study 2: 𝑡 (138) > 9.7, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 > 0.822).
text.formatted: In both studies, participants categorized training and test items more accurately than expected by chance (50%) in every run, including the first session (one-sample t-tests; Study 1: 𝑡 (61) > 6, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 > 0.763; Study 2: 𝑡 (138) > 9.7, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 > 0.822).

text.text: Differences from chance were substantial.
This suggests that generalizable knowledge about the underlying concepts formed in the first session already.
Importantly, conceptual knowledge continued to improve across tasks and sessions.
This was suggested by the fact that categorization accuracy increased across successive training and test runs in both studies (Fig. 2A and B).
text.formatted: This was suggested by the fact that categorization accuracy increased across successive training and test runs in both studies (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2A</ref> and <ref type="figure">B</ref>).

text.text: We assessed these changes using linear mixed-effects models that accounted for repeated measurements within participants.
Run number (1-30 for training; 1-9 for testing) was included with linear and quadratic terms, allowing learning trajectories to curve rather than assuming a constant rate of improvement.

F-tests assessing the combined linear and quadratic effects of run number indicated significant changes in accuracy in both studies (Study 1, training: 𝐹 (2, 112.366) = 329.873, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.854; test: 𝐹 (2, 102.630) = 24.487, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.323; Study 2, training: 𝐹 (2, 262.940) = 1314.194, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.909; test: 𝐹 (2, 238.984) = 60.636, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.337), with larger effect-size estimates for training than testing.

We assessed when across days participants reached their individual peak performance levels in training and test runs.

We hypothesized that if correct categorization of test items mainly relies on successfully memorized training exemplars, participants should reach peak performance at test at roughly the time when performance peaks in training.

However, if additional memory processes are required to promote generalization -such as the integration of exemplar memories into abstract prototype representations -performance on test items may reach its maximum later than performance during training.
To test these alternative hypotheses, we compared the timing of peak performance between training and test runs.
For this, we identified the session in which each participant achieved their highest categorization accuracy, separately for training and test runs.

Test performance peaked later than training performance in both studies (Fig. 3; main effect of task, Study 1: 𝐹 (1, 118) = 6.398, 𝑝 = .013, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.051; Study 2: 𝐹 (1, 137) = 59.747, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.304).
text.formatted: Test performance peaked later than training performance in both studies (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3</ref>; main effect of task, Study 1: 𝐹 (1, 118) = 6.398, 𝑝 = .013, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.051; Study 2: 𝐹 (1, 137) = 59.747, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.304).

text.text: In Study 1, this difference depended on training-set size (interaction between task and training-set size: 𝐹 (1, 118) = 9.889, 𝑝 = .002, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.077).

Post-hoc comparisons with Holm adjustment showed that test performance peaked significantly later than training performance for the small training set of eight items (𝑡 (59) = 3.892, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 = 1.023).
text.formatted: Post-hoc comparisons with Holm adjustment showed that test performance peaked significantly later than training performance for the small training set of eight items (𝑡 (59) = 3.892, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 = 1.023).

text.text: No significant difference was detected for the large training set of 24 items (𝑡 (59) = -0.453, 𝑝 Holm = .652, 𝑑 = -0.112).
In Study 2, test performance peaked later than training performance, with no significant evidence that the size of this delay differed between conditions (𝑝 > .325).
text.formatted: In Study 2, test performance peaked later than training performance, with no significant evidence that the size of this delay differed between conditions (𝑝 > .325).

text.text: However, the overall timing of peak performance differed between conditions: averaged across training and testing, peaks occurred earlier when additional category-irrelevant features were present than when stimuli contained only relevant features (main effect of condition: 𝐹 (1, 137) = 4.163, 𝑝 = .043, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.029).
These findings suggest that the ability to generalize to test items reaches its peak later than performance on training items.
Hence, the memory processes that promote generalization may continue to unfold even when training performance has already plateaued.
However, this may only be true when concepts are learned from small training sets.
In fact, the difference in peak times was observed only for the small training set in Study 1, and for both distinctiveness conditions in Study 2, where the training sets were always small.
In Study 1 (left panel), participants' performance peaked during earlier sessions for training vs. test runs, but only for the small training set (red).
In Study 2, training performance peaked in earlier sessions compared to test performance across both conditions.
Graphs present the grand means with 95% confidence intervals for the session number (1-5) in which participants' individual categorization accuracy reached the maximum for training and test runs.

text.text: The prototype model fitted participants' responses better than the exemplar model in all nine test runs in both studies (t-tests comparing model fit errors; Study 1: all 𝑡 (61) < -6, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 < -0.775; Study 2: all 𝑡 (138) < -6.696, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 < -0.567).

text.text: These differences were substantial, with 𝑑 < -0.775 in Study 1 and 𝑑 < -0.567 in Study 2; negative values indicate lower fit errors for the prototype model.

text.text: Importantly, the relative influence of prototype representations continued to increase over tasks and sessions in Study 1.

We assessed changes across the nine test runs using linear mixedeffects models that accounted for repeated measurements within participants and included linear and quadratic terms for run number, allowing trajectories to curve over time.

An F-test assessing the combined effects of these terms indicated a significant change in representational dominance, measured as prototype minus exemplar model fit error (𝐹 (2, 102.630) = 5.480, 𝑝 = .005, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.096).

In Study 2, changes in representational dominance depended on the presence of additional category-irrelevant features (see High perceptual distinctiveness impairs memory gen-eralization but promotes prototype dominance below).

In the high distinctiveness condition, which used the same stimuli as the small training set condition in Study 1, prototype dominance increased descriptively, but the corresponding F-test did not indicate a statistically significant change across runs (𝐹 (2, 116.294) = 1.535, 𝑝 = .220, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.026).
In both studies, model fit errors decreased across successive test runs, indicating that the cognitive models increasingly captured participants' categorization behavior.

F-tests assessing changes in model fit error with run number showed significant effects in both studies (Study 1: 𝐹 (2, 109.722) = 30.700, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.359; Study 2: 𝐹 (2, 256.483) = 66.701, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.342).
text.formatted: F-tests assessing changes in model fit error with run number showed significant effects in both studies (Study 1: 𝐹 (2, 109.722) = 30.700, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.359; Study 2: 𝐹 (2, 256.483) = 66.701, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.342).

text.text: This suggests that participants increasingly relied on category-relevant features for representing the learned concepts and for categorizing test items.
Additional control analyses suggested that the dominance of prototype representations is not an artifact of the stimulus material or the modeling approach.

Theoretically, it is conceivable that our modeling approach or the specific stimulus set we used allowed the prototype model to better fit any response pattern in the absence of a true prototype dominance.
For example, in our stimulus set, no single stimulus of the test set shared all relevant features with any of the training stimuli.
But multiple test stimuli perfectly matched their prototype.
This might provide an advantage for the prototype model.
On the other hand, exemplar models generally have greater flexibility and thus tend to provide better fits even to random response patterns [56].
text.formatted: On the other hand, exemplar models generally have greater flexibility and thus tend to provide better fits even to random response patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref>.

text.text: We therefore performed multiple control analyses to assess whether the observed representational dominance reflects a true dominance of prototype representations rather than stimulus-or modeling-inherent biases.

These analyses included leave-one-out cross-validations, Monte Carlo simulations, the fitting of mixture models that estimate the relative influence of exemplar and prototype models under the assumption that both can simultaneously guide behavior, and fitting prototype and exemplar models using psychologically plausible multimodal embeddings [57] instead of binary features to represent the stimulus material.
text.formatted: These analyses included leave-one-out cross-validations, Monte Carlo simulations, the fitting of mixture models that estimate the relative influence of exemplar and prototype models under the assumption that both can simultaneously guide behavior, and fitting prototype and exemplar models using psychologically plausible multimodal embeddings <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref> instead of binary features to represent the stimulus material.

text.text: In all these control analyses, the overall pattern of results remained unchanged.

Specifically, we observed an overall dominance of prototype representations, as well as an increase in prototype dominance across tasks and sessions (for details, see Validation of the computational modeling approach).
Standard theories of human memory posit that memory abstraction and the extraction of conceptual knowledge can occur offline following learning, especially during periods of rest.

We therefore examined how conceptual knowledge evolved offline in our studies by assessing the change in categorization behavior between the last training or test run of a session (before the offline period) and the first run of the next session on the next day (after the offline period; see Fig. 4 and supplementary Figs. S1 and S2).
text.formatted: We therefore examined how conceptual knowledge evolved offline in our studies by assessing the change in categorization behavior between the last training or test run of a session (before the offline period) and the first run of the next session on the next day (after the offline period; see Fig. <ref type="figure">4</ref> and supplementary Figs. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">S1</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">S2</ref>).

text.text: Specifically, we assessed how the representational dominance (exemplar vs. prototype) evolved offline.
We further examined changes in categorization accuracy and response times for both training and test runs.
Participants' internal representations shifted towards prototypes during offline periods.

This was suggested by an analysis of the influence of time (pre-vs. post-offline assessment) on the representational dominance, i.e., the difference between the model fit errors for prototype vs. exemplar models.
In Study 1, representational dominance significantly shifted towards prototypes from the pre-to the post-offline period (main effect of time: 𝐹 (1, 413) = 6.179, 𝑝 = .013, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.015).

There was some indication that this shift differed between training-set sizes, although the interaction between time and training-set size did not reach statistical significance (𝐹 (1, 413) = 3.458, 𝑝 = .064, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.008).

Post-hoc comparisons detected a significant shift towards prototypes for the small training set (𝑡 (413) = 2.980, 𝑝 Holm = .006, 𝑑 = 0.391), whereas no significant shift was detected for the large training set (𝑡 (413) = 0.455, 𝑝 Holm = .649, 𝑑 = 0.056).

In Study 2, a similar shift towards prototypes was observed in the high distinctiveness condition, which used the same stimulus set as the small training set condition in Study 1 (effect of time: 𝐹 (1, 469) = 4.624, 𝑝 = .032, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.010, 𝑑 = 0.184).
The estimated effect was smaller than in Study 1.
No significant shift was detected in the low distinctiveness condition (𝐹 (1, 490) = 0.184, 𝑝 = .668, 𝜂 2  𝑝 < .001).
text.formatted: No significant shift was detected in the low distinctiveness condition (𝐹 (1, 490) = 0.184, 𝑝 = .668, 𝜂 2  𝑝 < .001).

text.text: Interestingly, categorization accuracy did not show significant offline changes for either test or training items.

This was suggested by analyses in which we assessed categorization accuracy as a function of time (pre-/post-offline), task (training/test) and experimental conditions (training set size and motivational context in Study 1, distinctiveness in Study 2).
In both studies, time (pre-/post) did not significantly modulate accuracy, either as a main effect or in interaction with any other predictor (all 𝑝 > .128).
text.formatted: In both studies, time (pre-/post) did not significantly modulate accuracy, either as a main effect or in interaction with any other predictor (all 𝑝 > .128).

text.text: Following these nonsignificant results, we conducted an exploratory analysis asking whether observed accuracy increases were more frequent across offline intervals for test than for training items, irrespective of the magnitude of change.
For each participant and interval, we classified accuracy changes as increases or no increases, with the latter including unchanged or decreased accuracy.
We then used binomial generalized linear mixed-effects models to assess whether the odds of an observed increase differed by task and experimental condition.
In this exploratory analysis, increases were significantly more frequent for test than for training items in the conditions that also showed significant shifts towards prototype representations.
This finding concerns the frequency of observed increases rather than their magnitude and does not establish an average offline improvement in accuracy.

In Study 1, the difference between training and testing in how frequently accuracy increased across offline intervals depended on training-set size (interaction between time and condition: 𝜒 2 (1) = 5.687, 𝑝 = .017; interaction odds ratio, OR = 0.388).

Post-hoc comparisons showed that, for the small training set, the odds of an interval showing increased accuracy were approximately 2.9 times as high for test as for training runs (OR = 2.911, 𝑧 = 3.676, 𝑝 Holm < .001).
text.formatted: Post-hoc comparisons showed that, for the small training set, the odds of an interval showing increased accuracy were approximately 2.9 times as high for test as for training runs (OR = 2.911, 𝑧 = 3.676, 𝑝 Holm < .001).

text.text: For the large training set, no significant difference was detected (OR = 1.130, 𝑧 = 0.451, 𝑝 Holm = .652).
A similar pattern was observed in Study 2 in the high distinctiveness condition, which used the same stimulus set as the small training set condition in Study 1.
In this condition, the odds of an offline interval showing increased accuracy were approximately 2.6 times as high for test as for training runs (𝜒 2 (1) = 22.044, 𝑝 < .001, OR = 2.574).
text.formatted: In this condition, the odds of an offline interval showing increased accuracy were approximately 2.6 times as high for test as for training runs (𝜒 2 (1) = 22.044, 𝑝 < .001, OR = 2.574).

text.text: No significant difference between test and training runs was detected in the low distinctiveness condition (𝜒 2 (1) = 0.541, 𝑝 = .462, OR = 1.145).
To illustrate these effects, we plotted the mean number of offline periods during which participants showed a gain in accuracy separately for each task, condition, and study (Fig. 4).
text.formatted: To illustrate these effects, we plotted the mean number of offline periods during which participants showed a gain in accuracy separately for each task, condition, and study (Fig. <ref type="figure">4</ref>).

text.text: Importantly, response latencies showed offline drifts that were consistent with the observation of a shift of internal representations: In both studies, response latencies increased significantly after an offline period for training but not for test items.
In Study 1, an F-test indicated a small but significant three-way interaction between time (pre-vs. post-offline), task, and training-set size (𝐹 (1, 885) = 4.680, 𝑝 = .031, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.005).
Responses were generally slower during training than testing (effect of task: 𝐹 (1, 885) = 142.035, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.138).
text.formatted: Responses were generally slower during training than testing (effect of task: 𝐹 (1, 885) = 142.035, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.138).

text.text: Post-hoc comparisons detected a significant offline slowing for training runs in the small training set condition (𝑡 (885) = -4.081, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 = -0.536; negative values reflect the pre-minus-post contrast).
text.formatted: Post-hoc comparisons detected a significant offline slowing for training runs in the small training set condition (𝑡 (885) = -4.081, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 = -0.536; negative values reflect the pre-minus-post contrast).

text.text: No significant offline changes were detected for test runs in this condition or for either task in the large training set condition (|𝑡 (885)| < 0.766, 𝑝 Holm > .999, all |𝑑| < .095).
text.formatted: No significant offline changes were detected for test runs in this condition or for either task in the large training set condition (|𝑡 (885)| < 0.766, 𝑝 Holm > .999, all |𝑑| < .095).

text.text: In Study 2, offline changes in response times differed between training and testing in both distinctiveness conditions.
In the high distinctiveness condition, an F-test indicated a significant interaction between time and task (𝐹 (1, 1005) = 4.975, 𝑝 = .026, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.005).

Post-hoc comparisons detected significant offline slowing for training runs (𝑡 (1005) = -2.383, 𝑝 Holm = 0.035, 𝑑 = -0.204), whereas no significant change was detected for test runs (𝑡 (1005) = 0.7716, 𝑝 Holm = 0.441, 𝑑 = 0.066).
A similar pattern was observed in the low distinctiveness condition, with a significant interaction between time and task (𝐹 (1, 1050) = 12.155, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.011).
text.formatted: A similar pattern was observed in the low distinctiveness condition, with a significant interaction between time and task (𝐹 (1, 1050) = 12.155, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.011).

text.text: Post-hoc comparisons detected significant offline slowing for training runs (𝑡 (1050) = -4.016, 𝑝 Holm < 0.002, 𝑑 = -0.337), but no significant change for test runs (𝑡 (1050) = 0.915, 𝑝 Holm = 0.361, 𝑑 = 0.077).
text.formatted: Post-hoc comparisons detected significant offline slowing for training runs (𝑡 (1050) = -4.016, 𝑝 Holm < 0.002, 𝑑 = -0.337), but no significant change for test runs (𝑡 (1050) = 0.915, 𝑝 Holm = 0.361, 𝑑 = 0.077).

text.text: As in Study 1, negative effect sizes reflect slower responses after the offline interval because contrasts were calculated as preminus post-offline values.
We next examined whether offline changes in representational dominance, categorization accuracy, and response times were associated within participants.
We focused on the small training set condition in Study 1 and the high distinctiveness condition in Study 2, where significant offline shifts towards prototype representations had been detected.

In both studies, repeated-measures correlations showed that, within participants, offline intervals with larger shifts towards prototype representations were associated with larger increases in test accuracy (Study 1: 𝑟 rm = -.531; Study 2: 𝑟 rm = -.294; both 𝑝 Holm < .001).
text.formatted: In both studies, repeated-measures correlations showed that, within participants, offline intervals with larger shifts towards prototype representations were associated with larger increases in test accuracy (Study 1: 𝑟 rm = -.531; Study 2: 𝑟 rm = -.294; both 𝑝 Holm < .001).

text.text: The negative correlations reflect the coding of representational dominance: more negative changes indicate larger shifts towards prototypes.
The corresponding associations with changes in training accuracy were not statistically significant (Study 1: 𝑟 rm = .042, 𝑝 Holm > .999; Study 2: 𝑟 rm = -.179, 𝑝 Holm = .094).
text.formatted: The corresponding associations with changes in training accuracy were not statistically significant (Study 1: 𝑟 rm = .042, 𝑝 Holm > .999; Study 2: 𝑟 rm = -.179, 𝑝 Holm = .094).

text.text: In Study 1, larger offline increases in training accuracy were also associated with larger increases in training response times (𝑟 rm = .378, 𝑝 Holm = .003).
No other correlations reached statistical significance (all 𝑝 Holm > .183).
text.formatted: No other correlations reached statistical significance (all 𝑝 Holm > .183).

text.text: Thus, offline shifts towards greater prototype dominance were associated with changes in generalization accuracy, despite the absence of a significant average offline increase in accuracy.
In sum, our results suggest that conceptual knowledge continues to evolve offline, between daily experimental sessions.

Although prototype models better explained categorization from the first assessment, their relative advantage increased further across offline intervals in the small training set condition in Study 1 and the high distinctiveness condition in Study 2.

Within these conditions, larger offline shifts towards prototype dominance were associated with larger increases in test accuracy, despite the absence of a significant average offline improvement in accuracy.
An exploratory analysis also found that observed accuracy increases were more frequent for test than for training items in these conditions.
Response times increased offline for training items in the small training set condition in Study 1 and in both distinctiveness conditions in Study 2.

Together, these findings suggest that offline changes involve the continued refinement of existing prototype-based representations, with larger shifts towards prototype dominance associated with larger increases in generalization accuracy.

In Study 1 (A) in the small training set condition (red; "small"), we observed offline changes in behavior that indicate an offline transformation of conceptual knowledge.
Specifically, we observed that representations shifted towards prototypes (Repr.

Dom.: difference in representational dominance, post-minus pre-offline period), observed accuracy increases were more frequent for test than for training runs (Freq. incr.: number of offline intervals during which accuracy showed any increase, irrespective of its magnitude), and response latencies increased for training but not test runs (Resp. time: difference in response latencies, post-minus pre-offline period).
Importantly, we replicated these results in Study 2 (B) in the high distinctiveness condition (red; "high").
Grand mean values with 95% confidence intervals are plotted.
In Study 1, we examined how concept knowledge evolves when learning builds on a very limited set of experiences compared to a larger set of distinct experiences.

Specifically, we asked how training performance, test performance, representational dominance, and response latencies evolve across runs and sessions when participants practice with only 8 compared to 24 distinct training items (small vs. large training set).
Importantly, the number of training opportunities was held constant across conditions by repeating stimuli in the small training set three times per training run.
A larger training set did not yield a detectable advantage in concept generalization (Fig. 5).
text.formatted: A larger training set did not yield a detectable advantage in concept generalization (Fig. <ref type="figure">5</ref>).

text.text: Neither mean accuracy on the generalization test nor its evolution across runs and sessions differed significantly between training-set conditions (effect of training-set size: 𝐹 (1, 59) = 1.332, 𝑝 = .253, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.022; interaction with run number: 𝐹 (2, 102.630) = 1.104, 𝑝 = .336, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.021).
No significant effects of training-set size were detected for representational dominance (all 𝑝 > .112), model fit errors (all 𝑝 > .237), or response times during testing (all 𝑝 > .083; Fig. S3).
text.formatted: No significant effects of training-set size were detected for representational dominance (all 𝑝 > .112), model fit errors (all 𝑝 > .237), or response times during testing (all 𝑝 > .083; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">S3</ref>).

text.text: During training, however, participants in the large training set condition were less accurate overall (effect of training-set size: 𝐹 (1, 59) = 9.419, 𝑝 = .003, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.138), and their accuracy improved more slowly across runs (interaction between training-set size and run number: 𝐹 (2, 112.366) = 6.737, 𝑝 = .002, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.107).
Response times also decreased more slowly during training in the large training set condition (interaction: 𝐹 (2, 112.366) = 6.434, 𝑝 = .002, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.103).

In the featureknowledge test administered after the final session, participants in the large training set condition recalled fewer category-specific feature values (𝜒 2 (1) = 7.306, 𝑝 = .007, OR = 1.516 for small relative to large training sets).
Recognition accuracy, however, did not differ significantly between training-set conditions (𝐹 (1, 52) = 0.525, 𝑝 = .472, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.010).

In sum, increasing the number of distinct training examples while holding the total number of training presentations constant did not yield a detectable advantage in generalization accuracy or significantly promote prototype dominance.

This could suggest that successful generalization and internal representations of concepts (exemplar vs. prototype) are mainly determined by the number of training opportunities (which was identical across conditions), not the diversity of experiences (which was larger in the large training set).
Interestingly, participants trained with the larger set showed lower training accuracy and slower improvements during training.
These differences likely reflect the fewer repetitions of each individual training example in the larger set.
It is still possible that the size of training sets influences the trajectory of concept learning.
In fact, we observed better recall of category-defining feature values in the small compared to the large training set condition.

We also detected a significant offline shift towards greater prototype dominance in the small but not the large training set condition (see Conceptual knowledge evolves offline between daily experimental sessions).

Finally, we observed that generalization accuracy progressed more slowly in the small training condition (see Conceptual knowledge progresses more slowly than knowledge about specific training exemplars).
Categorization accuracy for training items improved more slowly for the large and more diverse training set compared to the small set (A).
However, neither categorization accuracy at test (B) nor model fits (C) nor representational dominance (D) were significantly influenced by training set size.
Grand mean values with 95% confidence intervals are plotted.
In Study 2, we assessed how perceptual distinctiveness influences concept learning.

We compared learning performance and the relative fit of exemplar and prototype models between stimuli containing both category-relevant and category-irrelevant features (high distinctiveness) and stimuli containing only category-relevant features (low distinctiveness).
Participants in the high distinctiveness condition achieved higher training accuracy and improved more rapidly across training runs (Fig. 6).
text.formatted: Participants in the high distinctiveness condition achieved higher training accuracy and improved more rapidly across training runs (Fig. <ref type="figure">6</ref>).

text.text: F-tests indicated significant effects of condition on training accuracy (𝐹 (1, 137) = 8.824, 𝑝 = .004, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.061) and an interaction between condition and run number (𝐹 (2, 262.940) = 6.435, 𝑝 = .002, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.047).

During testing, however, participants in this condition showed lower categorization accuracy (𝐹 (1, 137) = 27.405, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.167) and larger model fit errors (𝐹 (1, 137) = 31.881, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.189).
text.formatted: During testing, however, participants in this condition showed lower categorization accuracy (𝐹 (1, 137) = 27.405, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.167) and larger model fit errors (𝐹 (1, 137) = 31.881, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.189).

text.text: The evolution of representational dominance also differed between conditions, with a significant interaction between condition and run number (𝐹 (2, 238.984) = 9.811, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.076).
text.formatted: The evolution of representational dominance also differed between conditions, with a significant interaction between condition and run number (𝐹 (2, 238.984) = 9.811, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.076).

text.text: In the high distinctiveness condition, no significant change in prototype dominance was detected across test runs (𝐹 (2, 116.294) = 1.535, 𝑝 = .220, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.026).
In the low distinctiveness condition, prototype dominance decreased significantly over time (𝐹 (2, 121.545) = 14.231, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.190).
text.formatted: In the low distinctiveness condition, prototype dominance decreased significantly over time (𝐹 (2, 121.545) = 14.231, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.190).

text.text: Nevertheless, the prototype model fitted categorization responses better than the exemplar model at every test in both conditions (t-tests: all 𝑝 Holm < .003, all 𝑑 < -0.371).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, the prototype model fitted categorization responses better than the exemplar model at every test in both conditions (t-tests: all 𝑝 Holm < .003, all 𝑑 < -0.371).

text.text: Direct comparisons between conditions at the first test in session 1 and the last test in session 5 further illustrated these different trajectories.
At the first test, prototype dominance was significantly greater in the low distinctiveness condition (𝑡 (135.791) = -2.381, 𝑝 Holm = .019, 𝑑 = -0.403).
At the last test, the direction of the difference was reversed, with significantly greater prototype dominance in the high distinctiveness condition (𝑡 (128.061) = 3.074, 𝑝 Holm = .005, 𝑑 = .523).
No significant effects of condition on response times were detected (all 𝑝 > .071).
text.formatted: No significant effects of condition on response times were detected (all 𝑝 > .071).

text.text: Participants in the high distinctiveness condition also showed better knowledge of categorydefining feature values in the feature-knowledge test administered after the final session (Fig. S5).
text.formatted: Participants in the high distinctiveness condition also showed better knowledge of categorydefining feature values in the feature-knowledge test administered after the final session (Fig. <ref type="figure">S5</ref>).

text.text: The odds of correctly recalling a feature value and assigning it to the corresponding family were approximately 25% higher in the high than in the low distinctiveness condition (𝜒 2 (1) = 5.629, 𝑝 = .018, OR = 1.246).

Participants in the high distinctiveness condition also identified the family associated with individual feature values more accurately in the recognition task (𝐹 (1, 133) = 4.760, 𝑝 = .031, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.035).

These results suggest that high perceptual distinctiveness facilitates memorization of individual training examples, but also promotes prototype learning and the generation of explicit insights into category-defining features, while paradoxically reducing generalization to test items not presented during training.
High perceptual distinctiveness (highlighted in red) facilitated learning of training items as indicated by increased accuracy during training runs (A).
However, high distinctiveness impaired the transfer to test items (B; lower accuracy) and thus interfered with concept learning.
Relatedly, high distinctiveness was associated with worse model fits (C).
Prototype dominance decreased over time in the low distinctiveness condition, whereas no significant change was detected in the high distinctiveness condition (D).
Prototype models fitted responses better than exemplar models at every assessment in both conditions (negative values in D).
Grand mean values with 95% confidence intervals are plotted.
We examined how abstract, generalizable knowledge for naturalistic concepts is acquired and evolves over multiple days.
For this, we had participants learn to categorize high-dimensional, multimodal cartoon monsters into two families (the concepts) in daily sessions over five consecutive days.
We assessed participants' abilities to generalize their knowledge to items not presented during training and fitted cognitive models of category learning to categorization behavior.
Participants rapidly generalized in the first session already, and their knowledge continued to improve with further training over the next days.

Cognitive modeling suggested that concepts were represented by abstract prototypes rather than memories for unique training exemplars, and that the dominance of prototype representations increased with further training.
Importantly, conceptual knowledge continued to evolve offline between test sessions, outside of actual training and test tasks.
Specifically, the dominance of prototype representations increased offline.

Moreover, observed accuracy increases across offline intervals were more frequent for test than for training items, whereas response latencies slowed offline selectively for training but not test runs.
Our concept learning task promoted the use of prototype rather than exemplar representations for categorizing new items.
Importantly, this prototype dominance tended to increase across learning.
Even when concepts were learned with only a few instead of many training exemplars (8 vs.
24), prototype dominance persisted.

This is relevant because learning with the smaller training set facilitated the memorization of training exemplars, which in theory should have promoted the use of these exemplars rather than prototypes for categorizing new items at test.

Our results thus are in stark contrast to a large body of evidence which suggests that concepts tend to be represented by means of specific memorized exemplars [8, 12, [58] [59] [60], that the influence of exemplar representations increases with training [22, 23], and that small training sets promote exemplar dominance [44, 45].
text.formatted: Our results thus are in stark contrast to a large body of evidence which suggests that concepts tend to be represented by means of specific memorized exemplars <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[58]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[59]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60]</ref>, that the influence of exemplar representations increases with training <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23]</ref>, and that small training sets promote exemplar dominance <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45]</ref>.

text.text: However, previous work almost unanimously used low-dimensional, unimodal stimuli that contained only category-relevant features, and studied concept learning in single-session experiments only.

We argue that the observed prototype dominance in our studies was due to our use of perceptually unique, multi-modal, high-dimensional stimuli that contained both relevant and irrelevant perceptual features.
Removing the irrelevant features in the low distinctiveness condition in Study 2 indeed changed the dominance of prototype representations.
When irrelevant features were present, prototype dominance was strong (both studies) and increased across learning (Study 1).
When these features were removed (Study 2), prototype dominance was even stronger in the beginning but decreased across learning, as participants formed robust memories for the training exemplars.
This latter finding closely matches earlier reports which suggested that exemplar dominance increases with training [22, 23].
text.formatted: This latter finding closely matches earlier reports which suggested that exemplar dominance increases with training <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23]</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the presence of category-irrelevant features facilitated learning of training exemplars but impaired generalization to items not presented during training -despite promoting the use of prototype representations at test.

This finding may seem paradoxical: How can excellent memory for training exemplars still allow for the formation of prototype representations and encourage the use of these prototypes for categorizing new items?

We argue that the high distinctiveness provided by the presence of category-irrelevant features not only facilitated learning of training exemplars but also increased the discriminability between training and test items.
Note that each cartoon monster had a unique physical appearance as well as a unique pronounceable name.
No two monsters looked alike -even when sharing all category-relevant features.
Due to the high distinctiveness between training and test items, participants did not try to directly compare test items to individual training exemplars.
Instead, they identified and used abstract rules or prototypes for categorizing new items at test.
But they may sometimes have included irrelevant features in their prototype definitions, leading to lower performance at test.
This argumentation is supported by studies which suggested that the presence of category-irrelevant features generally impairs categorization [52] [53] [54] but promotes formation of prototypes [13].
text.formatted: This argumentation is supported by studies which suggested that the presence of category-irrelevant features generally impairs categorization <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[52]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref> but promotes formation of prototypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Our argumentation further finds support in the observation that exemplar and prototype representations may coexist in the brain [21], and may be used strategically in different contexts.
text.formatted: Our argumentation further finds support in the observation that exemplar and prototype representations may coexist in the brain <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>, and may be used strategically in different contexts.

text.text: Conceptual knowledge continued to evolve offline between sessions.
Specifically, concept representations shifted further towards prototypes from the last task of a session to the first task of the next session on the following day.
Moreover, categorization accuracy showed a higher ratio of offline gains for test compared to training accuracy, and response latencies showed offline slowing for training but not test runs.
These findings suggest that offline periods promoted the refinement of abstract and integrated concept representations that were less dependent on the memory for specific training exemplars.

Importantly, these significant offline shifts towards prototypes were only observed for the small but not the large training set condition (Study 1), where concept learning was based on only a few distinct training examples (8 instead of 24).
In the small training set, the covariance between the perceptual features that are relevant for categorization was less diverse.

This may hinder the extraction of abstract, generalizable rules for categorizing new items during training due to overfitting and may call for post-learning memory processes that enable generalization and insight.

Additionally, significant offline shifts towards prototypes were observed only for the highly distinct stimuli that contained category-irrelevant perceptual features, not for the low distinctiveness stimuli that only contained category-relevant features (Study 2).
High dimensionality may have impeded identification of relevant features and may have promoted overfitting, which again called for post-learning processing to enable generalization.
We argue that offline transformation of conceptual knowledge was enabled by mechanisms that promote memory consolidation during periods of rest and sleep following learning [25] [26] [27] [28].
text.formatted: We argue that offline transformation of conceptual knowledge was enabled by mechanisms that promote memory consolidation during periods of rest and sleep following learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: During rest and sleep, the brain is believed to replay previously acquired memories [29, 30], promoting their integration and the extraction of abstract, generalized representations.
text.formatted: During rest and sleep, the brain is believed to replay previously acquired memories <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30]</ref>, promoting their integration and the extraction of abstract, generalized representations.

text.text: This consolidation account is consistent with the observation that offline transformations occurred only in the small, but not the large, training-set condition, that is, when fewer training examples were repeated more often (18 rather than 6 times per session).
A recent study showed that repetition during encoding increases the likelihood of subsequent offline replay [61], which in turn may promote generalization and abstraction [62].
text.formatted: A recent study showed that repetition during encoding increases the likelihood of subsequent offline replay <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[61]</ref>, which in turn may promote generalization and abstraction <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">[62]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, repeated exposure to the same training examples may have increased their probability of offline reactivation and thereby facilitated the transformation of category knowledge.

However, because we neither monitored sleep nor tracked spontaneous offline reactivation of memories, we cannot determine whether such consolidation processes were responsible for the observed transformations.
Other mechanisms could have contributed as well.
For example, selective forgetting of detailed information about the training examples might account for the observed offline changes [63].
text.formatted: For example, selective forgetting of detailed information about the training examples might account for the observed offline changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">[63]</ref>.

text.text: Individual training exemplars and irrelevant details are generally more prone to forgetting than abstract prototypes [64, 65].
text.formatted: Individual training exemplars and irrelevant details are generally more prone to forgetting than abstract prototypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">[64,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">65]</ref>.

text.text: Assuming that exemplar and prototype representations coexist in the brain [20, 21], selective forgetting of exemplar-specific information may therefore have increased the relative influence of prototype representations on subsequent categorization behavior.
text.formatted: Assuming that exemplar and prototype representations coexist in the brain <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21]</ref>, selective forgetting of exemplar-specific information may therefore have increased the relative influence of prototype representations on subsequent categorization behavior.

text.text: Alternatively, participants may have deliberately searched for rules and regularities defining category membership between sessions, potentially leading to insights that boosted performance on the following day.
Such explicit search and optimization may have been encouraged by the deferred feedback on average categorization performance provided after each test run [66].
text.formatted: Such explicit search and optimization may have been encouraged by the deferred feedback on average categorization performance provided after each test run <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">[66]</ref>.

text.text: The present data therefore cannot distinguish whether offline transformations arose from spontaneous memory-consolidation processes, differential forgetting, active post-session reflection, or a combination of these mechanisms.
Admittedly, our findings are not without limitations.

Although we used naturalistic highdimensional stimuli and a multi-day study design to track the long-term emergence of conceptual knowledge in a more realistic setting than previous studies, our findings may still not fully translate to concept learning in everyday life.
For example, we repeatedly used the same training and test stimuli across sessions.
But in everyday life, conceptual knowledge often evolves from unique experiences, and it needs to generalize to many unseen events.
The generalizability of our findings is further limited by the fact that we clearly labeled training and test tasks.
But in everyday life, the distinction between familiar and novel experiences may not always be clear.

The transferability of our findings is also limited by the specific concept structure used in our work: participants learned simple, linearly separable categories that contained no exceptions to the rules.
But natural concepts often have complicated hierarchical, non-linearly separable structures that include unique exceptions and rare cases.
Finally, our primary cognitive-model analyses included only the predefined category-relevant features.
This does not directly impair the validity of our findings because irrelevant features were fully counterbalanced across the concepts.
However, it limits the generalizability to everyday learning, where experiences are always high-dimensional, and irrelevant features are not counterbalanced across learning examples.

Our work advances our understanding of how humans integrate high-dimensional, multimodal experiences into abstract generalized representations that allow us to make sense of new events and situations.
We show that even when only a limited set of training examples is available, repeated training can provide abstract knowledge that generalizes to new situations.
The emergence of this knowledge benefits from extensive training even when training performance is already at ceiling.
Moreover, this knowledge may continue to evolve offline, possibly during periods of rest and sleep.

These findings are consistent with proposed benefits of spaced vs. massed learning: repeated re-learning, testing and feedback across multiple sessions that are distributed over time can enhance long-term retention of the learning material [67] and support memory generalization and abstraction [68], yielding new conceptual knowledge.
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with proposed benefits of spaced vs. massed learning: repeated re-learning, testing and feedback across multiple sessions that are distributed over time can enhance long-term retention of the learning material <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">[67]</ref> and support memory generalization and abstraction <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">[68]</ref>, yielding new conceptual knowledge.

text.text: In order to participate in our studies, volunteers had to be native or near-native German (both studies) or French (Study 2) speakers and had to have normal or corrected-to-normal hearing levels and vision.
Moreover, individuals had to have regular sleep schedules during the time of study participation (no shift work).
Only individuals who reported no sleep disorders, no diagnosed memory deficits, and no current episodes of schizophrenia or depression were invited to participate.
Data were excluded from analysis if participants failed to comply with the study protocol.
Main reasons for exclusion were missed or incomplete sessions, taking two sessions in one day, or delaying sessions by one or more days.

Data were further excluded if a participant's categorization accuracy never significantly exceeded chance level (50%), based on a cutoff derived from the binomial distribution (one-tailed, 𝛼 = .025), for any of the training or test runs.
Finally, data were excluded if a participant's categorization accuracy across all training or test runs was < 50%.
text.formatted: Finally, data were excluded if a participant's categorization accuracy across all training or test runs was < 50%.
