text.text: In Study 1, the experimental manipulations training set size (small vs. large) and motivational context (gamified vs. neutral) were implemented as a 2×2 between-subjects design.
In Study 2, the experimental condition distinctiveness (high: stimuli include relevant and irrelevant features vs. low: relevant features only) was implemented as a between-subjects factor.
In both studies, four different stimulus sets with distinct prototypes and stimuli were used in different subsets of participants, counterbalanced across conditions.
Stimulus set was treated as a nuisance variable and was not included as a factor in our analyses.
General procedure Volunteers signed up for participation via email or through our participant management system.
They then received an email with a link to the consent form and to demographic and pre-screening questionnaires.

Volunteers who met the inclusion criteria were randomly assigned to one of the experimental conditions and were then asked by email to indicate their preferred starting date for participating in the five daily sessions.
At 5:00 a.m. on each scheduled testing day, participants received an email with the link to the experimental session of the current day.

Participants were allowed to complete sessions at their preferred time of day, but were instructed to take each session at about the same time of day, in the same quiet environment, and on the same device (computer or tablet; no smartphones).
Each session started with a brief sleep questionnaire and then proceeded to the actual experiment.
Before continuing with the experiment, a brief audio test was administered to ensure that participants could hear the sound on their computer or tablet.
Then, the cover story and instructions for the experiment were presented.

Each experiment started with a generalization test, during which we assessed how well participants could transfer their knowledge from the previous sessions to a set of 64 test items that were never shown during training.
This test was omitted in the first session.
Next, participants took six feedback-based training runs of 24 trials each.
After the second and fourth training runs, brief interim tests with 8 items that were never shown during training or generalization tests were administered.
These interim tests aimed at motivating participants to form abstract concept representations.
After training run 6, a second generalization test was administered.
After each training and test run, participants were informed about their average accuracy during the previous run.
Participants were allowed to take a short break before continuing with the next task.
The context of each task (training/test) was announced before the start.
The experiment ended with a brief questionnaire that assessed the intrinsic motivation to participate in the experiment.
On the last day, an additional feature knowledge test was administered to assess participants' knowledge of the perceptual features characterizing each monster family.
Finally, the participants were debriefed and compensated.

Pre-screening questionnaire Upon signing up for participation, volunteers completed a prescreening questionnaire in which they were asked about their age, level of education, current occupation, and language skills.

In this questionnaire, participants were also asked to disclose the current presence of neurological or psychiatric disorders (namely epilepsy, depression, schizophrenia), attention or memory deficits, hearing or vision impairments, sleep disorders, or irregular sleep schedules, e.g., due to shift work.
A French translation was provided to French-speaking participants in Study 2.

At the beginning of each session, participants' subjective sleepiness and the quality of their last night's sleep were assessed using the German version [69] of the Karolinska sleepiness scale [70], the German version [69] of the Epworth sleepiness scale [71], and a single-item sleep quality scale [72].
text.formatted: At the beginning of each session, participants' subjective sleepiness and the quality of their last night's sleep were assessed using the German version <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">[69]</ref> of the Karolinska sleepiness scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">[70]</ref>, the German version <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">[69]</ref> of the Epworth sleepiness scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">[71]</ref>, and a single-item sleep quality scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">[72]</ref>.

text.text: For French-speaking participants in Study 2, all questionnaire items were translated into French.
At the end of each session, participants' motivation to partake in the experiment was assessed using the short German version of the intrinsic motivation inventory [73].
text.formatted: At the end of each session, participants' motivation to partake in the experiment was assessed using the short German version of the intrinsic motivation inventory <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">[73]</ref>.

text.text: For French-speaking participants in Study 2, the questionnaire was translated into French.
This scale consists of four subscales that are measured with three items each.
The interest/enjoyment subscale assesses how fun and engaging the task is.
It is the most direct self-report measure of intrinsic motivation.
The competence scale assesses how effective, skilled, or capable a person feels when performing the task.
The choice scale relates to autonomy and indicates the sense of freedom to perform the task.
The pressure/tension scale indicates the feeling of stress or coercion while performing the task.
It is assumed to be a negative predictor of intrinsic motivation.

Participants were told that in this experiment they must learn to categorize monsters called "Fernis" into two families, the "Brigus" and the "Sidors" that have distinctive sets of visual and auditory features.

Participants were instructed to try to identify the relevant features and feature combinations that define each monster family during training runs in order to maximize their categorization accuracy during both training and test runs.
The cover story of the experiment was that a bunch of monster babies had just hatched from their eggs in a forest where Fernis go to breed.
These hatchlings now need to find their way home to their families.

The participants' task was to learn to identify Brigus and Sidors during training runs so that they can then tell the hatchlings in test runs which family they belong to and where they find their home.
Training runs Each trial during training started with a blank screen that was presented for a jittered duration of 500 to 1000 ms.
Then, a monster was displayed on the screen, and its name was played in its own voice over loudspeakers.
Participants had to indicate the family of the monster on display by clicking on the button of the corresponding family (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Participants had to indicate the family of the monster on display by clicking on the button of the corresponding family (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The monster was displayed until a participant responded.
Upon response, feedback on the accuracy of the response was provided.
For correct responses, a rewarding jingle sound was played, and a happy smiley face and a green check mark were displayed in front of a green rectangle.
For incorrect responses, an annoying horn sound was played, and a sad smiley face and a red cross mark were shown in front of a red rectangle.
The feedback screen was presented for a fixed duration of 2000 ms.
Then, the task proceeded to the next trial.
In each of the 6 training runs in a session, 24 items were presented in pseudo-random order.

In the experimental conditions where participants practiced with 8 training examples (small set condition in Study 1, all conditions in Study 2), the 8 items were repeated three times in each training run.
Items were repeated in blocks and were presented in a new pseudo-random order for each repetition within a run.
In the condition where participants practiced with 24 training examples (large set condition in Study 1), each item was presented only once per run.
This yielded a total of 144 training opportunities (24 item presentations × 6 runs) in each session.
The sequence of events during test runs was identical to the sequence during training runs (a blank screen followed by a monster stimulus), but no feedback was provided upon response.
In each generalization test run, the same set of 64 test items that were never shown during training was presented in pseudo-random order.
At the very end of the last experimental session, a feature knowledge test was administered which probed participants' knowledge of the category-defining perceptual features.
In this test, we first examined whether participants were able to recall the defining feature values of each monster family.
For this, we asked participants to list the defining feature values of each monster family in an open-ended question.
Then we assessed whether participants could recognize the family that is associated with each feature value of the eight binary features.
For this, each feature value was presented on screen one by one (e.g., a picture of monster arms, along with the text label "arms") in pseudo-random order.
For each value, participants had to indicate the corresponding family by clicking the respective button on the screen.
No feedback was provided.
This task consisted of 16 trials (two feature values for each of the 8 binary features).
Half of the participants in Study 1 were subjected to a gamified version of the concept learning task.
In this version, participants were told that they would compete against six other participants who were also performing the task.
They were informed that correct responses are rewarded with a point and that they should try to outcompete their opponents by collecting the most points.
The opponents were in fact virtual players whose behavior dynamically adapted to each participant's current performance level in order to keep the task demanding yet rewarding.
However, participants were misled into believing that their opponents were actual human participants.
This deception was approved by the ethics committee.
At the beginning of each session, the six opponents were introduced with brief vignettes and avatars.
Participants were told that they would compete against one of these opponents during each training run, but that they would compete against all six opponents at once during test runs.
Before each training run, the opponent for the next run was introduced.
Participants were told that they would see their own score and the opponent's score after each trial.
The presentation of training trials was identical to that in the non-gamified, neutral condition.

However, the feedback screens that were provided after each response contained information about the accuracy of both the participant's and the opponent's last response and about each player's total score.
At the end of a training run, a leaderboard was displayed which showed whether the participant or the opponent won the last run.

Before each test run, participants were informed that they would now have to compete against all six opponents, that no feedback would be presented after a response, but that a leaderboard would be shown at the end.
The sequence of events was identical to that in the test runs in the non-gamified, neutral condition.
Whenever a participant won a training or test run, the sound of a cheering crowd was played and the avatar of the player received a trophy.
When participants did not win a round, a sad sound was played and the text "You can do better!"
was displayed below the leaderboard.

Stimulus properties Stimuli consisted of cartoon monsters that differed on six visual and two auditory binary features that were relevant for categorization.
The features and their values are listed in Table 1.
text.formatted: The features and their values are listed in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: The cartoon monsters further differed on a set of features that were not relevant for categorization because the different values within each feature were counterbalanced across families.
These irrelevant features included the lightness of the body color (4 levels), the body type (skinny vs.

heavyset, 4 levels), the skin texture (unique set of randomly generated dark skin spots), the type of thorns (4 types: sine waves, triangles, squares, spikes), the length (4 levels) and density (4 levels) of thorns, the hairdo (unique shape), the lightness of the hair color (4 levels of green), the positions of the body parts (the upper and lower extremities, eyes, and oral structure could each vary across 4 levels of vertical position, horizontal position, and orientation), and the name suffix (unique pronounceable three-syllable pseudo-word).
Hence, each monster had a unique visual appearance and a unique name.
Monsters' names always started with one of two possible prefixes ("NINI" or "DADA") of the relevant binary name feature, and ended with a unique three-syllable suffix (e.g., "kitome").
Monsters' names were presented acoustically and were uttered in one of two possible voices (binary feature voice).
For the low distinctiveness condition in Study 2, one fixed value for each of these additional features was used for all monsters.
Drawings of cartoon monsters were generated by combining hand-drawn images of body parts with computer-generated images of the main body and hair on a square canvas of 1000 × 1000 pixels.
Monsters were scaled to a height of 500 pixels on that canvas.

Audio files for the presentation of the monster names were synthesized using an Italian female voice ("it-IT-Wavenet-B") and a male US voice ("en-US-Neural2-D") from the Google Cloud Text-To-Speech (TTS) API (https://cloud.google.com/text-to-speech).
text.formatted: Audio files for the presentation of the monster names were synthesized using an Italian female voice ("it-IT-Wavenet-B") and a male US voice ("en-US-Neural2-D") from the Google Cloud Text-To-Speech (TTS) API (<ref type="url" target="https://cloud.google.com/text-to-speech">https://cloud.google.com/text-to-speech</ref>).

text.text: The two monster families were defined by orthogonal prototypes with distinct values for all eight category-defining binary features.
From these prototypes, stimuli with varying prototypicality were derived by changing 0, 1, 2, or 3 of the features to the value corresponding to the prototype of the opposite family.
The training set consisted of either four stimuli (small set in Study 1, both conditions in Study 2) or 12 stimuli (large training set in Study 1) per family.
Each stimulus differed from its category prototype by two features (prototypicality of 75%).
The interim test set consisted of four stimuli per family that all had a prototypicality of 75%.
The test set consisted of 32 stimuli per family.
Test stimuli differed from their prototype by either 0, 1, 2, or 3 features, with 8 stimuli per level of deviation.

The test set thus included 8 stimuli per family that had prototypical category-defining features but that varied in their individual irrelevant features (except for the low distinctiveness condition in Study 2, where irrelevant features were absent).
The rate at which features deviated from the prototype was identical across features and within families and sets (training, interim test, test).
Hence, all features had the same diagnostic value.
Feature combinations were never repeated across training, interim test, and test (except for the 8 prototypical stimuli for each category in the test set).
Feature combinations were manually defined for the Brigu family only and were then derived for the Sidor family by inverting all features to the opposite value.
A full list of stimulus definitions for the Brigu family is provided in the supplementary tables S2 , S3, and S4.
We generated four different stimulus sets that were each defined by different pairs of orthogonal prototypes.
The prototypes for the Brigu family of each set are presented in Table 2.
text.formatted: The prototypes for the Brigu family of each set are presented in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>.

text.text: The corresponding opposite prototypes for the Sidor family were obtained by inverting each binary feature value (e.g., {1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1} for the Sidor prototype for Set 0).
Individual stimuli were then generated using the same logic as for set 0, i.e., by inverting specific feature values from the prototype as listed in supplementary tables S2 , S3, and S4.
Feature values correspond to the binary feature coding described in Table 1.

text.text: We fitted formal models of exemplar-and prototype-based concept representations to participants' behavior in the generalization test.
The prototype model posits that humans form one abstract, prototypical representation for storing a concept.
New items are classified as members of that category if they exhibit high perceived similarity to the stored prototype.
In contrast, the exemplar model assumes that humans categorize by comparing new items to specific examples stored in memory.
A new item is classified into a category if the sum of the perceived similarities to all memorized examples of that category is high.

In both models, perceived similarity depends not only on physical similarity (e.g., the number of shared features) but also on the attention given to each feature (attentional weights 𝑤) and the discounting of items with low perceptual similarity (sensitivity 𝑐 in an exponential decay function).

To quantify how well a model with specific values for 𝑤 and 𝑐 predicts a participant's behavior, we calculated a negative log-likelihood error measure by taking the negative of the sum of the logarithms of the estimated probabilities that the model assigns each item 𝑥 𝑖 to the same category as the participant: where 𝑛 is the total number of test items, 𝑅 𝑗 is the participant's response to item 𝑥 𝑗 , i.e., the category (𝐴 or 𝐵) to which they assigned the item, and 𝑃(𝑅 𝑗 |𝑥 𝑗 ) is the model's predicted probability that 𝑥 𝑗 belongs to the category assigned by the participant.

To fit a model to a participant's behavior, we optimized the parameters 𝑐 and 𝑤 to obtain a minimal model fit Error, i.e., to find the best possible prediction of behavior based on stimulus features and model assumptions.
Feature weights were constrained to be positive and sum to one.
Sensitivity was bounded between 10 -12 and 700.
Parameters were optimized using the L-BFGS-B algorithm implemented in R's optim function [76].
text.formatted: Parameters were optimized using the L-BFGS-B algorithm implemented in R's optim function <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">[76]</ref>.

text.text: The resulting error value was used as an index for how well each model can predict behavior.
The model with the better fit (lower error) was assumed to dominate behavior.

Representational dominance was thus defined as: where negative values indicate dominance of prototype representations, positive values indicate exemplar dominance, and 0 suggests no clear dominance or equal fits.
Model fitting was conducted in R [76], using custom code inspired by Bowman [77].
text.formatted: Model fitting was conducted in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">[76]</ref>, using custom code inspired by Bowman <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">[77]</ref>.

text.text: Models were fitted to the single-trial data of test runs separately for each participant and each single test run (pre-and post-training test runs for each session; 9 fits per model per participant).
In the primary analyses, models were fitted using only the 8 binary features relevant for categorization.
The irrelevant features were ignored.
The reasons for this were manifold.
First, we were interested in how well participants learned to identify and use relevant features in order to categorize items.
Moreover, the irrelevant features were generally less salient, less verbalizable, and were counterbalanced across families for both training and test items.
They were thus truly non-diagnostic of families and are therefore treated as random noise.
Importantly, the irrelevant features were introduced to create a more naturalistic setting where each exemplar of a family represents a unique, memorizable identity (e.g., the names).
The features were not created with the intention of using them for model fitting.

In fact, they were not suitable for use with our model fitting procedure, because they were sometimes not binary but ordinal or categorical, were undefined for the abstract prototypes, and were overall too large in number.
Moreover, the raw features used for stimulus generation could interact non-linearly to create unique perceptual properties.
Hence, they did not necessarily represent clearly distinct one-dimensional perceptual properties -unlike the diagnostic binary features.
Some participants appeared to reverse the family labels in individual generalization tests, resulting in performance significantly below chance.
They rapidly corrected their mistake in the first training run that followed.

We identified these participants and tasks based on the following rules: accuracy in the task was significantly below chance level (𝑝 < .001) according to a binomial test, and accuracy deviated by more than 2 standard deviations from the average accuracy in all other test runs.
text.formatted: We identified these participants and tasks based on the following rules: accuracy in the task was significantly below chance level (𝑝 < .001) according to a binomial test, and accuracy deviated by more than 2 standard deviations from the average accuracy in all other test runs.

text.text: For these tests, we reversed the two family labels in participants' responses and recalculated accuracy.
To assess the evolution of categorization accuracy across tasks and sessions, we calculated the ratio of correct responses separately for each task, run, and session for each participant.
To analyze response latencies, we calculated the median response time for correct responses within each run and applied a log10 transformation to these medians.

To contrast the time of peak performance between training and test runs, we identified the session number (1-5) in which each participant reached the highest categorization accuracy separately for training and test runs.

To examine whether conceptual knowledge evolved offline, we assessed how categorization accuracy, response latencies, model fits, and representational dominance changed from the last task of a session to the first task of the next session.
For these analyses, we only kept the data from the last training runs (run 6) and test tasks of sessions 1 to 4, and from the first training runs and test tasks of sessions 2 to 5.
We then labeled the tasks based on their time of administration relative to the offline periods (pre-or post-offline task) and based on the specific offline period (1-4).
In an exploratory analysis, we also counted, separately for training and testing, the number of offline intervals during which each participant's accuracy increased.
Any positive change was classified as an increase, whereas unchanged or decreased accuracy was classified as no increase.
This measure captures the frequency of observed increases irrespective of their magnitude.

To assess participants' knowledge of the category-defining features, we counted the number of correctly recalled feature values for each category from the open-ended questions of the feature knowledge task.
We predefined a coding framework to perform a deductive content analysis of participants' open-ended descriptions of the defining features of each category.

This allowed us to count the total number of correctly recalled features, which yielded a feature recall score ranging from 0 (no features were recalled) to 16 (all feature values were recalled and correctly attributed to the corresponding category).
We additionally calculated feature recognition accuracy as the ratio of single feature values that were correctly attributed to the corresponding category in the ensuing item-by-item test.

Task number ranged from 1 to 30 for training runs (5 sessions with 6 runs each), and from 1 to 9 for test runs (first session with one test, sessions 2 to 5 with 2 tests each).

To contrast the time of peak performance between training and test runs, we performed linear mixed model analyses with the session number (1-5) indicating each participant's time of peak performance as the dependent variable, with task (training vs. test), condition, and their interaction as fixed effects, and with random intercepts for participants:

text.text: While we approve of the logic behind the use of Monte Carlo simulations, we believe that the proposed implementation has one big disadvantage: the permutation of participants' responses controls for their response biases (i.e., how often they preferred one response over the other), but not for their response accuracy.
But accuracy has a strong systematic influence on model fits and the difference between model fits, whereas response bias does not (Fig. S6).
text.formatted: But accuracy has a strong systematic influence on model fits and the difference between model fits, whereas response bias does not (Fig. <ref type="figure">S6</ref>).

text.text: In fact, model fits nonlinearly improve with response accuracy in both true and simulated or permuted data, and the differences in model fits show an increasing dominance of exemplar models with increasing accuracy.
Importantly, randomly shuffling participants' responses tends to lead to response patterns with lower accuracy, and hence worse model fits and biased distributions of the differences in model fits.

To overcome this limitation, we implemented an alternative permutation-based approach to correct for model-and stimulus-inherent biases: (1) we simulated multiple random response patterns at all possible levels of response accuracy (1000 per accuracy level, or as many as possible; total number of data sets: 𝑁 = 61131), (2) fitted both models to each random data set, (3) computed the distributions for the differences between model fits at each accuracy level, and (4) normalized each observed difference in model fits by the distribution of differences drawn from random response patterns at the accuracy level of the true data.
Normalization consisted of subtracting the mean simulated dominance at the corresponding accuracy level and training-set size, and dividing by its simulated standard deviation.
We then used this permutation-normalized representational dominance to validate our original findings.
The distributions of model fits and the differences in model fits calculated for the simulated random response patterns are displayed as a function of response accuracy and response bias in Fig. S6.

In Study 1, we also aimed to investigate how the motivational context shapes the acquisition of novel concepts.

In everyday life, concept learning is often motivated by goals: Humans are motivated to acquire new concepts because this knowledge enables them to understand and act effectively in relevant situations.
The motivational context in which learning occurs may therefore influence how rapidly and successfully a concept is acquired, and potentially how it is represented.

Consistent with this possibility, some studies have found that rewarding correct categorizations, rather than providing neutral corrective feedback, facilitates concept learning [84, 85] and promotes the formation of prototype representations [86].
text.formatted: Consistent with this possibility, some studies have found that rewarding correct categorizations, rather than providing neutral corrective feedback, facilitates concept learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">[84,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">85]</ref> and promotes the formation of prototype representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">[86]</ref>.

text.text: However, other studies have found no evidence for superior learning under reward-based compared with neutral conditions [87, 88].
text.formatted: However, other studies have found no evidence for superior learning under reward-based compared with neutral conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">[87,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">88]</ref>.

text.text: How motivational context influences the long-term development of conceptual knowledge therefore remains poorly understood.
We examined the role of motivation by comparing concept learning in gamified and neutral contexts.

Gamification -which involves adding game elements such as points, rewards, and leaderboards to non-game contexts -has been found to increase motivation [89] and improve learning outcomes across a variety of settings [90] [91] [92] [93].
text.formatted: Gamification -which involves adding game elements such as points, rewards, and leaderboards to non-game contexts -has been found to increase motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">[89]</ref> and improve learning outcomes across a variety of settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">[90]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">[91]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">[92]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">[93]</ref>.

text.text: Yet, to the best of our knowledge, whether gamification influences motivation and the acquisition and representation of conceptual knowledge has not been investigated.
In Study 1, half of participants were subjected to a gamified version of the concept learning task, in which they had to compete against other virtual participants during training and testing.
Participants in the control group performed the task without the additional competitive game elements.

At the end of each experimental session, we assessed participants' intrinsic motivation to perform the experimental tasks using a short version of the intrinsic motivation inventory [73] that builds on Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory [94].
text.formatted: At the end of each experimental session, we assessed participants' intrinsic motivation to perform the experimental tasks using a short version of the intrinsic motivation inventory <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">[73]</ref> that builds on Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">[94]</ref>.

text.text: This scale measures participants' perceived interest in and enjoyment of the task, the perceived competence at performing the task, the freedom of choice to participate in the task, and the perceived pressure or tension when performing the experiment.
Gamification elements failed to improve intrinsic motivation (Fig. S7).
text.formatted: Gamification elements failed to improve intrinsic motivation (Fig. <ref type="figure">S7</ref>).

text.text: Overall, participants' interest in the tasks decreased across sessions (main effect of session: 𝐹 (2, 88.368) = 17.887, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.288), indicating a loss of motivation to continue with the experiment.
text.formatted: Overall, participants' interest in the tasks decreased across sessions (main effect of session: 𝐹 (2, 88.368) = 17.887, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.288), indicating a loss of motivation to continue with the experiment.

text.text: However, the perceived competence increased (𝐹 (2, 86.945) = 16.795, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.279), while the perceived pressure decreased (𝐹 (2, 82.379) = 24.560, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.374).
text.formatted: However, the perceived competence increased (𝐹 (2, 86.945) = 16.795, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.279), while the perceived pressure decreased (𝐹 (2, 82.379) = 24.560, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.374).

text.text: No significant change in freedom of choice was detected (𝐹 (2, 87.351) = 1.284, 𝑝 = .282, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.029).
Interestingly, participants who learned the concepts in a gamified context generally reported lower interest in the task (main effect of context: 𝐹 (1, 58.897) = 5.427, 𝑝 = .023, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.084).
This suggests that gamification undermined intrinsic motivation.

However, participants in the gamified condition also showed a steeper decline in the perceived pressure across sessions (interaction between context and session: 𝐹 (2, 82.378) = 4.948, 𝑝 = .009, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.107).
This could indicate either a more indifferent attitude towards the task, as is also indicated by the lower general interest, or greater familiarity or reduced anxiety.
Competence and freedom of choice were not significantly modulated by the motivational context (gamified vs. neutral: all 𝑝 > .174).
text.formatted: Competence and freedom of choice were not significantly modulated by the motivational context (gamified vs. neutral: all 𝑝 > .174).

text.text: Importantly, gamification had no significant impact on concept learning (Fig. S8 and S9).
text.formatted: Importantly, gamification had no significant impact on concept learning (Fig. <ref type="figure">S8</ref> and <ref type="figure">S9</ref>).

text.text: Neither training nor test accuracy, nor model fits or representational dominance were significantly modulated by the context (gamified vs. neutral; all 𝑝 > .068).
text.formatted: Neither training nor test accuracy, nor model fits or representational dominance were significantly modulated by the context (gamified vs. neutral; all 𝑝 > .068).

text.text: However, response latencies during testing (𝐹 (1, 59) = 5.939, 𝑝 = .018, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.091) but not training (all 𝑝 > .292) were significantly shorter in the gamified condition.
text.formatted: However, response latencies during testing (𝐹 (1, 59) = 5.939, 𝑝 = .018, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.091) but not training (all 𝑝 > .292) were significantly shorter in the gamified condition.

text.text: This more rapid responding might reflect facilitated accessibility or processing efficiency of the acquired conceptual knowledge.
Alternatively, it could also mirror the overall lower interest in the task.

To assess this possibility, we added within and between participant variation in intrinsic interest as predictors of response latencies across generalization tests, adjusting for session and experimental conditions.
The effect of gamification remained significant (𝐹 (1, 56.706) = 4.652, 𝑝 = .035, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.076) when controlling for interest.
Moreover, participants responded more slowly in sessions when their reported interest was higher than their own average (𝐹 (1, 392.310) = 16.645, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.041).
text.formatted: Moreover, participants responded more slowly in sessions when their reported interest was higher than their own average (𝐹 (1, 392.310) = 16.645, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.041).

text.text: No significant association was detected between participants' average interest and response latencies (𝐹 (1, 58.761) = 0.294, 𝑝 = .590, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.005).
Thus, the association between gamification and faster test responses persisted after adjustment for reported interest.
Faster responding may reflect facilitated access to conceptual knowledge or greater processing efficiency, although the present analyses do not establish the underlying mechanism.
In sum, using a gamified environment failed to generally improve motivation and learning success.
These findings suggest that the particular combination of game elements used here did not improve task interest or categorization accuracy.

text.text: Model fit errors systematically decreased for random response patterns with higher response accuracies (A) but fit errors were not systematically modulated by response bias (B).
Moreover, differences in model fits showed an increasing dominance of exemplar representations for simulated data with high response accuracies (C).
Differences were not systematically modulated by response bias (D).
Accuracy is expressed as the ratio of correct responses in simulated data.
Bias is expressed as the ratio of responses given to the preferred category, where 0.5 indicates perfectly balanced responses, and 1.0 indicates preference for only one category.

However, the approach can be influenced by differences in model flexibility: a more flexible model may achieve a better fit by accommodating idiosyncratic response variability rather than by providing a better account of a participant's underlying concept representation.
We therefore complemented our primary analyses with leave-one-out cross-validation.
For each test trial, we estimated model parameters from all remaining trials and then predicted the participant's response on the held-out trial.
For each held-out trial, we quantified prediction error as the negative logarithm of the probability assigned by the model to the participant's observed response.

Cross-validated model error was then calculated as the mean prediction error across all held-out trials: where 𝑃(𝑦 𝑖 | 𝑥 𝑖 , θ-𝑖 ) is the probability that the model assigns to the response 𝑦 𝑖 the participant actually made on trial 𝑖, using the model parameters θ-𝑖 estimated from all trials except trial 𝑖.
Lower values therefore indicate better out-of-sample prediction of participants' responses.

We then calculated the cross-validated representational dominance parameter from the Error CV computed for the exemplar and prototype models to validate our findings on the dominance of prototype representations.

Comparing predictive performance across held-out trials provides an out-of-sample assessment of the relative explanatory power of the prototype and exemplar models that is less susceptible to differences in model flexibility.

Instead of comparing the fit errors of separately fitted exemplar and prototype models, an alternative approach involves fitting a mixture model that assumes both types of representations can simultaneously contribute to behavior, but with different degrees of influence.

We therefore defined two mixture models which assume that both prototype-and exemplarbased representations can contribute to categorization, with a parameter 𝛼 determining their relative influence: where 𝛼 = 0 only considers the prototype model, 𝛼 = 1 only considers the exemplar model, and 𝛼 = 0.5 considers both models equally.
𝑃 ex ( 𝐴 | 𝑥) and 𝑃 pr ( 𝐴 | 𝑥) are the probabilities that a new item 𝑥 belongs to category 𝐴 according to the exemplar or prototype model, respectively.

Importantly, we defined two models: one that assumes that exemplar and prototype representations have distinct feature weights 𝑤 and sensitivities 𝑐 (the distinct-weights model with 𝛼 distinct as the model preference parameter derived from model fitting), and one that assumes only distinct 𝑐 parameters, but shared weights 𝑤 (the shared-weights model with 𝛼 shared ) for exemplar and prototype representations.
Both models were fitted by finding optimal parameters for 𝛼, 𝑤, and 𝑐 to yield the smallest possible model fit error (see eq.
The shared-weights model was also fitted to the simulated data, which allowed us to calculate a normalized 𝛼 shared z parameter from the parameter distribution obtained from simulated data.
We used these additional parameters (𝛼 distinct , 𝛼 shared , 𝛼 shared z ) to validate our original findings on the dominance of the prototype model.
For our primary analyses, we fitted exemplar and prototype models using the eight pre-defined diagnostic binary features.
This approach ignored the additional category-irrelevant features.
But these additional features are what make each stimulus unique.

Ignoring these features might thus lead to a disadvantage of the exemplar model, which assumes that all individual training exemplars are stored in memory and are used to categorize new items based on their similarity on all perceptual features.

To represent both relevant and irrelevant perceptual features of the stimuli in a psychologically meaningful way, we extracted multimodal embeddings (visual and auditory) by passing the images and sound files of each monster through the pre-trained multimodal embedding model ImageBind [57].
text.formatted: To represent both relevant and irrelevant perceptual features of the stimuli in a psychologically meaningful way, we extracted multimodal embeddings (visual and auditory) by passing the images and sound files of each monster through the pre-trained multimodal embedding model ImageBind <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref>.

text.text: This yielded 1024 embeddings for each modality (visual, auditory, text), which we reduced using principal component analysis (PCA).
We selected the 12 visual, 2 auditory, and 2 text principal components with the highest variability as features to represent each stimulus.

Importantly, representational similarity analyses suggested that these 16 embedding features reliably encoded the stimulus structure (i.e., the pairwise dissimilarities between stimuli) provided by the binary features (𝑟 > 0.666 for all stimulus sets).
text.formatted: Importantly, representational similarity analyses suggested that these 16 embedding features reliably encoded the stimulus structure (i.e., the pairwise dissimilarities between stimuli) provided by the binary features (𝑟 > 0.666 for all stimulus sets).

text.text: Moreover, binomial ridge regressions confirmed that the monster family could be decoded with high accuracy using the embedding features (AUC > .999 for all stimulus sets).
text.formatted: Moreover, binomial ridge regressions confirmed that the monster family could be decoded with high accuracy using the embedding features (AUC > .999 for all stimulus sets).

text.text: Hence, embedding features accurately represented the binary features while presumably also representing additional perceptually salient information that is not accounted for when using the binary features only for model fitting.
We used the 16 embedding features to separately fit the exemplar and prototype models to behavior and then calculated the embedding-derived representational dominance.
For the continuous embedding-derived features, we used 𝑟 = 2 as the distance metric (see eq. 1 and 2).
The prototype representations were calculated by averaging each feature across all participant-specific training stimuli of the same family.
We used the embedding-derived representational dominance to validate our original findings on the dominance of the prototype model.
In our primary analyses, we compared the fit errors to assess whether the exemplar or the prototype model better accounts for the data.
While this is standard practice, model errors are somewhat non-intuitive and may be sensitive to the model-specific magnitude/scaling of the predicted probabilities.

This makes comparing model fits difficult when different numbers of trials are used or different numbers and types of features are used for model fitting (e.g., when comparing model fit errors for models fitted with the full data and binary features to model fit errors from cross-validation or models fitted with normally distributed embeddings).
In order to obtain a more intuitive and directly comparable metric of model fit, we additionally quantified how accurately each model predicted participants' categorical choices.
For each trial, the category assigned the higher probability by the fitted model was taken as the model's predicted response: where 𝑁 denotes the number of trials.
Ties received half credit for models fitted to all trials and no credit for leave-one-out cross-validated predictions.

Unlike model error based on the negative log-likelihood, this prediction accuracy is insensitive to the magnitude of the predicted probabilities as long as their ordering remains unchanged, and therefore provides a complementary and readily interpretable measure of how well a model captures participants' categorical choices.

From the prediction accuracies computed for the exemplar and prototype models, we calculated the prediction accuracy-derived representational dominance parameter to validate our findings on the dominance of prototype representations.
We combined the above approaches to calculate a total of 11 additional representational dominance parameters, presented alongside the primary measure in Table S1.
text.formatted: We combined the above approaches to calculate a total of 11 additional representational dominance parameters, presented alongside the primary measure in Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>.

text.text: Eight of these parameters replicated the observed dominance of prototype representations for both studies.
Note that the two parameters derived from cross-validated fit errors showed Only the embedding-derived parameters from models fitted to all trials showed no clear model preference.
But the prototype dominance was present for the embedding-based parameters calculated using leave-one-out cross-validation.

Importantly, the cross-validated representational dominance calculated using the model fit error showed no model dominance for Study 1, and a clear exemplar dominance for Study 2, for the low distinctiveness condition.
However, the dominance parameter calculated from the response prediction accuracy displayed a clear prototype dominance for both studies.

text.text: However, it is also possible that we used a suboptimal combination of game elements for our study.

Especially competitive settings and leaderboards, as used in our study, were repeatedly found to adversely affect learning and motivation in studies investigating the use of gamification in educational software [96].
text.formatted: Especially competitive settings and leaderboards, as used in our study, were repeatedly found to adversely affect learning and motivation in studies investigating the use of gamification in educational software <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">[96]</ref>.

text.text: Finally, it is possible that the neutral, non-gamified version of the task already contained game-like elements that typically boost motivation and learning.
In the neutral condition, we used engaging narrative elements to introduce the experiment ("help cartoon monsters find their home by learning to identify their family").
Such fiction elements were found to enhance learning [90].
text.formatted: Such fiction elements were found to enhance learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">[90]</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, we provided affectively valenced performance feedback instead of neutral corrective feedback during training: Correct and incorrect responses were followed by a positive jingle and a happy emoji or an aversive horn sound and a sad emoji, respectively.
Positive and negative feedback, compared to simple corrective feedback, can improve concept learning [97].

text.text: After the final session, participants completed a feature-knowledge test assessing recall and recognition of category-defining feature values.
In the recall task, participants described the features associated with each monster family in their own words.
Responses were scored out of 16 possible feature values: eight diagnostic features, each with two values associated with the two families.
Participants correctly recalled and assigned an average of 4.29 feature values in Study 1 (𝑛 = 55, SD = 4.00, median = 2) and 5.04 in Study 2 (𝑛 = 135, SD = 4.42, median = 4).
In the subsequent recognition task, participants identified the family associated with each individual feature value.

Mean recognition accuracy was 74.3% in Study 1 and 76.2% in Study 2, exceeding chance performance (50%) in both studies (one-sample t-tests; Study 1: 𝑡 (54) = 11.410, 𝑝 < .001, 𝑑 = 1.539; Study 2: 𝑡 (134) = 17.648, 𝑝 < .001, 𝑑 = 1.519).

Participants were recruited from the body of German-speaking (both studies) and French-speaking (Study 2) bachelor's students in psychology at UniDistance Suisse, Switzerland, as well as from the general population (Study 1 only).
Participation was rewarded with course credits for bachelor's students in psychology or with monetary compensation (CHF 90.-) for non-students.
Written consent was obtained from all individuals prior to their participation.
The studies were approved by the ethics committee of UniDistance Suisse, Switzerland (application number 2024-03-00001).
Visual and sound stimuli were rendered from pre-defined lists of feature combinations using custom-made Python code.

The raw features used for generating the stimuli as well as the final rendered image and sound files used in our experiments are provided in the accompanying project repository (see Data and materials availability).
